data.title: Stevens–Johnson syndrome / TEN — viva
data.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 30 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Stevens–Johnson syndrome / TEN** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define SJS and TEN and classify by BSA.**
- Severe life-threatening mucocutaneous reactions, mostly drug-induced, with extensive keratinocyte death (epidermal necrosis) and detachment
- SJS: <10% body surface area (BSA) detachment; SJS–TEN overlap: 10–30%; TEN: >30% (Bastuji-Garin classification)
- Lesions: widespread dusky/purpuric macules, flat atypical targets, blisters; ≥2 mucosal sites

**Q2. Common culprit drugs (India).**
- Antiepileptics — carbamazepine (commonest in India), phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine
- Allopurinol (high risk, HLA-B*58:01), sulphonamides (cotrimoxazole), nevirapine, NSAIDs (oxicams), fluoroquinolones, β-lactams, anti-TB drugs, sulfasalazine, dapsone
- Onset typically 4–28 days after starting the drug (first exposure)
- Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a non-drug cause in children; ~5% idiopathic

**Q3. What are the HLA associations?**
- HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) in Han Chinese, Thai, Malay and some Indian populations — US FDA advises screening before starting carbamazepine in at-risk ancestry
- HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol; HLA-A*31:01 with carbamazepine DRESS/SJS in Europeans and Japanese; HLA-B*13:01 with dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome

**Q4. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Drug (or metabolite) presented by specific HLA → activates drug-specific cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and NK cells (p-i concept, altered peptide repertoire)
- Keratinocyte apoptosis/necroptosis by granulysin (key mediator; levels correlate with severity), perforin–granzyme B, Fas–FasL, TNF-α, annexin A1
- Massive keratinocyte death → full-thickness epidermal necrosis and subepidermal split

**Q5. Clinical features.**
- Prodrome 1–3 days: fever, sore throat, conjunctivitis, malaise, painful skin (cutaneous pain is an early warning)
- Rash starts on face and upper trunk → spreads; dusky erythematous/purpuric macules and flat atypical targets that coalesce, flaccid blisters, sheets of detached skin ('wet cigarette paper')
- Nikolsky sign and Asboe-Hansen sign positive on erythematous skin
- Mucosa (>90%): haemorrhagic crusting of lips, oral erosions, purulent conjunctivitis/pseudomembranes, genital erosions; also respiratory and GI epithelium

**Q6. Write a short note on Nikolsky sign (PYQ).**
- Shearing pressure on apparently normal/ perilesional skin causes separation of the epidermis
- Positive in pemphigus (intraepidermal acantholysis), SSSS, TEN (on erythematous skin), also EB, bullous impetigo; negative in bullous pemphigoid
- Variants: Nikolsky I (marginal — at blister edge), Nikolsky II (on normal skin away), Asboe-Hansen (bulla spread), pseudo-Nikolsky (TEN — on erythematous skin only)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- EM major (typical/raised targets, acral, HSV, less mucosal and no extensive detachment)
- SSSS (children, superficial split, no mucosa, sterile blister, tender erythema, flexural accentuation)
- GBFDE, AGEP (pustules), DRESS, linear IgA bullous dermatosis (drug — vancomycin), paraneoplastic pemphigus, bullous lupus/TEN-like lupus, GVHD grade IV, toxic shock syndrome, phototoxic reaction, burns, Kawasaki disease, MIRM

**Q8. How do you identify the culprit drug?**
- Detailed drug chart with exact start dates; ALDEN algorithm (Algorithm of Drug causality for Epidermal Necrolysis — time delay, drug presence, prechallenge/rechallenge, dechallenge, drug notoriety, other causes; score ≥6 very probable)
- In vitro tests (lymphocyte transformation test, ELISpot granulysin) — research; rechallenge contraindicated; patch test low sensitivity

**Q9. Investigations.**
- Skin biopsy (frozen section for rapid diagnosis): full-thickness epidermal necrosis, subepidermal split, sparse dermal infiltrate; DIF negative (excludes autoimmune bullous)
- CBC, renal function, electrolytes, bicarbonate, glucose, LFT, albumin, CRP, blood/skin/urine cultures, chest X-ray, ABG
- Mycoplasma serology/PCR in children; HLA testing if relevant

**Q10. What is SCORTEN? (prognostic score)**
- Calculated within 24 h of admission and at day 3; one point each: age ≥40 years; associated malignancy; heart rate ≥120/min; epidermal detachment >10% BSA on day 1; serum urea >10 mmol/L (≈28 mg/dL BUN); serum glucose >14 mmol/L (252 mg/dL); serum bicarbonate <20 mmol/L
- Predicted mortality: 0–1: ~3%; 2: ~12%; 3: ~35%; 4: ~58%; ≥5: >90%

**Q11. Supportive management (the backbone).**
- Immediately stop the culprit (and all non-essential drugs) — earlier withdrawal improves survival
- Admit to burns unit/ICU if SCORTEN ≥3 or >10% detachment; barrier nursing, warm room (30–32 °C), air-fluidised bed
- Fluids: lower than burns (≈ 2 ml/kg/%BSA + maintenance), guided by urine output 0.5–1 ml/kg/h; electrolytes; nutrition by nasogastric tube (high-protein, early)
- Skin care: leave blisters in place (biological dressing), non-adherent dressings (paraffin gauze, silicone, Mepitel), avoid adhesive tapes, silver dressings; no prophylactic systemic antibiotics — cultures and treat sepsis
- Eyes: daily ophthalmology review, lubricants, topical steroid/antibiotic drops, lysis of synechiae, amniotic membrane transplantation for severe ocular disease
- Mouth: oral rinses, white soft paraffin to lips; genital care (prevent synechiae — vaginal moulds); analgesia; DVT prophylaxis; stress ulcer prophylaxis; respiratory monitoring

**Q12. Specific (immunomodulatory) therapy.**
- Cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/day for 7–10 days then taper — preferred first-line in our protocol and many Indian/European centres (inhibits CD8 T cell activation; studies show reduced mortality vs predicted SCORTEN)
- Systemic corticosteroids: early short pulse (e.g. dexamethasone/methylprednisolone) — controversial; many Indian centres use within the first 72 h
- Etanercept (TNF-α blocker) 25–50 mg SC single/two doses — RCT showed faster healing and lower mortality vs steroids
- IVIG (2–3 g/kg over 3–4 days) — conflicting evidence; combinations (steroid + IVIG) used
- Plasmapheresis, N-acetylcysteine (adjunct) — limited data
- Thalidomide is contraindicated (increased mortality in RCT)

**Q13. What are the acute and long-term complications?**
- Acute: sepsis (commonest cause of death — S. aureus, Pseudomonas), fluid/electrolyte imbalance, hypothermia, acute kidney injury, hypoalbuminaemia, ARDS/bronchial sloughing, GI bleeding, hepatitis, DVT/pulmonary embolism, ileus
- Long-term (in ~50%): eyes — dry eye, symblepharon, trichiasis, entropion, corneal scarring, blindness; skin — dyspigmentation, scarring, eruptive naevi, nail loss, hypohidrosis; mucosal — oral, oesophageal, urethral, vaginal strictures; lungs — bronchiolitis obliterans; psychological (PTSD)

**Q14. How do you prevent recurrence and educate?**
- Give a drug-allergy card/medical alert bracelet listing culprit and structurally related drugs (e.g. aromatic antiepileptics cross-react: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine — use levetiracetam/valproate)
- Report to pharmacovigilance (PvPI — ADR monitoring centre in India)
- HLA screening before high-risk drugs in at-risk groups; first-degree relatives may share HLA risk
- Start allopurinol at low dose, avoid unnecessary use (asymptomatic hyperuricaemia)

**Q15. How do you classify cutaneous adverse drug reactions?**
- Immediate (type I, IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
- Delayed T-cell (type IV): IVa — eczematous (Th1), IVb — DRESS/maculopapular with eosinophils (Th2), IVc — SJS/TEN, FDE (cytotoxic T cells), IVd — AGEP (neutrophil, IL-8)
- Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs): SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, GBFDE

**Q16. Compare DRESS with SJS/TEN briefly.**
- DRESS: latency 2–8 weeks, morbilliform rash with facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia/atypical lymphocytes, internal organ involvement (liver commonest), HHV-6 reactivation; RegiSCAR score; systemic steroids mainstay with slow taper
- SJS/TEN: latency 4–28 days, epidermal necrosis and mucositis, cytotoxic T cell mediated, SCORTEN for prognosis

**Q17. Prognosis.**
- Mortality: SJS ~1–5%, overlap ~10–15%, TEN 25–35% (higher in elderly, extensive disease, delayed drug withdrawal)
- Re-epithelialisation usually in 2–3 weeks; mucosal and ocular sequelae may be lifelong

**Q18. What is the latency period and why is it important?**
- Usually 4–28 days after starting a new drug (first exposure); rechallenge can cause reaction within 48 h; drugs started >8 weeks earlier or used safely for years are unlikely culprits (except dose change) — key in ALDEN

**Q19. Describe the eye care protocol in SJS/TEN.**
- Daily ophthalmology review from admission: preservative-free lubricants hourly, topical steroid drops (prednisolone acetate) and antibiotic drops, glass-rod sweeping/lysis of conjunctival adhesions, scleral shells/ symblepharon rings
- Amniotic membrane transplantation within first week for significant ocular surface sloughing — reduces chronic sequelae; long-term follow-up for dry eye, trichiasis, limbal stem cell deficiency

**Q20. What are the oral, genital and respiratory care measures?**
- Mouth: warm saline/ antiseptic (chlorhexidine) mouthwashes, anaesthetic gels/ benzydamine, steroid mouthwash, white soft paraffin to lips; soft or nasogastric feeds
- Genital: daily examination, potent topical steroid ointment, non-adherent dressings, vaginal dilators/ moulds to prevent synechiae; urinary catheter if needed
- Respiratory: monitor oxygen saturation, chest X-ray, early intubation if bronchial involvement (poor prognosis)

**Q21. What fluid regimen is used?**
- Less than burns because dermis is intact: about 2 ml/kg/% BSA detached in first 24 h (plus maintenance) or titrated to urine output 0.5–1 ml/kg/h; prefer crystalloids, add albumin if low; avoid fluid overload; peripheral lines through unaffected skin

**Q22. Why are prophylactic antibiotics not given?**
- They select resistant organisms and increase drug-reaction risk; instead take skin/ blood/ urine/ catheter-tip cultures every 48 h and treat promptly when sepsis signs appear (fever may be absent — watch for hypothermia, falling BP, confusion, rising glucose, falling urine output)

**Q23. Discuss the cyclosporine regimen and evidence.**
- 3–5 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses for 7–10 days then taper over a month — inhibits T-cell activation and granulysin release; multiple cohort studies and meta-analyses show lower mortality than predicted by SCORTEN; first-line in our protocol; monitor BP, renal function, electrolytes

**Q24. What is the role of systemic corticosteroids?**
- Controversial: early short high-dose pulses (dexamethasone 1.5 mg/kg/day for 3 days or methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days) may halt progression when given within 72 h; prolonged steroids increase sepsis and mortality; commonly combined with IVIG or cyclosporine in Indian practice

**Q25. What are the HLA screening recommendations?**
- HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine/ oxcarbazepine in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, Malaysian, Indonesian and some Indian ancestry; HLA-B*58:01 before allopurinol in Han Chinese, Korean, Thai, and those with CKD; HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir (hypersensitivity syndrome)

**Q26. Which drugs cause SJS/TEN in HIV patients?**
- Nevirapine (first 6–8 weeks), cotrimoxazole (prophylaxis), anti-TB drugs, fluconazole; HIV increases SJS/TEN risk up to 1000-fold; manage carefully when restarting ART (avoid nevirapine permanently)

**Q27. Paediatric SJS/TEN — causes and differences.**
- Drugs: sulphonamides, antiepileptics (phenobarbitone, carbamazepine, lamotrigine), paracetamol (debated), NSAIDs; infections — Mycoplasma (MIRM), HSV; lower mortality than adults; ocular sequelae equally serious

**Q28. Discuss SJS/TEN in pregnancy.**
- Risk to mother and fetus (preterm birth); supportive care in burns/ICU; avoid teratogenic immunomodulators; IVIG and steroids preferred; neonatal TEN possible; vaginal synechiae may complicate delivery

**Q29. How do you differentiate SSSS from TEN histologically and clinically?**
- SSSS: children/renal failure, tender erythema starting periorificially and flexures, superficial peeling, no mucosal involvement, Nikolsky positive on normal skin; split at granular layer (frozen section of peeled skin — only stratum corneum and granular layer); antibiotics
- TEN: drug history, mucosa involved, full-thickness epidermal necrosis on frozen section, deeper detachment; stop drug, burns-unit care

**Q30. What is the pharmacovigilance pathway in India?**
- Report the ADR to the nearest ADR Monitoring Centre under Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI, Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission) via suspected ADR reporting form/ ADR PvPI app or toll-free helpline; causality (WHO-UMC/Naranjo) documented

## Quick spotter facts
- Painful skin + purpuric flat targets + ≥2 mucosae after carbamazepine — SJS/TEN
- SCORTEN 7 points (age ≥40, cancer, HR ≥120, BSA >10%, urea >10, glucose >14, bicarbonate <20)
- HLA-B*15:02 — carbamazepine

## Note
Cyclosporine first-line follows our department decision; steroid use varies between centres.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (SJS/TEN); SCORTEN; ALDEN; Indian SJS-TEN consensus. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
